response.sql:
WITH account_transaction_counts AS (
  SELECT 
    a.account_id,
    c.town_city,
    COUNT(ft.transaction_id) AS transaction_count
  FROM Accounts a
  INNER JOIN Customers c ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
  LEFT JOIN Financial_Transactions ft ON a.account_id = ft.account_id
  WHERE c.town_city IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY a.account_id, c.town_city
),
averages AS (
  SELECT AVG(CAST(transaction_count AS DECIMAL(19,4))) AS avg_count
  FROM account_transaction_counts
),
town_totals AS (
  SELECT town_city, SUM(transaction_count) AS town_total
  FROM account_transaction_counts
  GROUP BY town_city
)
SELECT 
  atc.account_id,
  atc.town_city,
  atc.transaction_count,
  CAST(atc.transaction_count AS DECIMAL(19,4)) / tt.town_total AS share_of_town_transactions,
  CAST(atc.transaction_count AS DECIMAL(19,4)) / a.avg_count AS ratio_to_average
FROM account_transaction_counts atc
CROSS JOIN averages a
JOIN town_totals tt ON atc.town_city = tt.town_city
ORDER BY ratio_to_average DESC
LIMIT 10;

assumptions.assumption: The average transaction count is calculated across only accounts with valid customers and non-null town_city values, not across all accounts in the database. This treats the filtered accounts as the basis set for comparison rather than all accounts that may have missing customer or location data.
Accounts with zero transactions are included in the average calculation (via LEFT JOIN with Financial_Transactions and COUNT of transaction IDs, which yields 0 for unmatched accounts).

alternatives.interpretation: The average transaction count could be calculated across all accounts with valid customers (regardless of whether their town_city is null), with the output then filtered to show only those with non-null towns. This would result in a lower average (if many customers have null towns) and different ratios. The town totals and share calculations would remain the same.
